n: Early in his reign, Nebuchadnezzar has disturbing dreams that keep him awake. Ancient kings took dreams seriously as messages from the gods about their rule.

f.w: the second year of the reign of Nebuchadnezzar
f.g: About 603 BC; the date may be counted differently from Daniel 1’s three-year training.
He could not sleep.

n: The king summons every kind of expert in dreams and omens. Babylon was famous for its libraries of dream interpretation and astrology.

f.g: Those who practiced spells and charms.
Here a class of learned astrologer-priests.

n: The king says he is troubled and must know what the dream means.
The experts reply in Aramaic, the international language of the day. From here to the end of chapter 7, the book of Daniel itself is written in Aramaic rather than Hebrew.

f.g: Aramaic. Daniel 2:4b–7:28 is written in Aramaic in the original text.
A standard courtly greeting.

n: The king demands that they tell him both the dream and its meaning, or they will be torn limb from limb and their homes destroyed. “The thing is gone from me” likely means “my decision is firm.”

f.w: The thing is gone from me
f.g: Probably “This is my firm decree,” not “I have forgotten.”
A heap of rubble or refuse.

n: If they succeed, they will receive gifts, rewards, and honor. The king offers both carrot and stick.
The wise men ask again to hear the dream first.
The king accuses them of stalling, hoping his mood will change.

f.g: You are buying time.

n: His logic is sharp: if they can truly read the divine meaning, they can also tell him the dream. If they can’t, their interpretations are lies.

f.g: Until circumstances change.

n: The experts protest that no human being can do this and no king has ever demanded it.
They admit that only the gods could reveal it—and the gods don’t live among mortals. Unknowingly, they set the stage for Daniel to show that his God does reveal secrets to men.

f.w: except the gods, whose dwelling is not with flesh

n: Enraged, the king orders all of Babylon’s wise men executed.
Daniel and his friends, now counted among the wise men, are sought out to be killed.
Daniel responds to Arioch, the captain of the king’s guard, with tact and good judgment rather than panic.

f.g: Commander of the king’s bodyguard (literally “chief of the executioners”).

n: Daniel asks why the decree is so urgent, and Arioch explains the situation.

f.g: Urgent, harsh.

n: Daniel boldly asks the king for time, promising to give the interpretation—an act of faith before he knows the answer.
Daniel goes home and tells his three friends.
Together they plead with the God of heaven for mercy to reveal the secret. Facing death, their first response is united prayer.

f.w: desire mercies of the God of heaven

f.g: Aramaic raz—a hidden mystery revealed by God.

n: God reveals the dream to Daniel in a night vision. Daniel’s first act is to praise God.

f.w: Then Daniel blessed the God of heaven

n: Daniel’s hymn of praise begins: wisdom and power belong to God.
God controls history—He sets up and removes kings and gives wisdom to the wise. This is the theme of the whole book of Daniel.

f.w: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings
he giveth wisdom unto the wise

n: God reveals hidden things and knows what lies in darkness, because light lives with Him.
Daniel thanks “the God of my fathers” and includes his friends: God has made known what “we” asked. He gives the credit where it belongs.

f.w: O thou God of my fathers

n: Daniel’s first concern is to save the other wise men—even the pagan astrologers. He asks Arioch to stop the executions and take him to the king.
Arioch hurries Daniel in and takes some credit: “I have found a man.” He calls Daniel one of the captives of Judah.
The king asks Daniel directly whether he can reveal both dream and meaning.
Daniel begins by agreeing that no human expert could do this.

f.g: Diviners or fortune-tellers.

n: But there is a God in heaven who reveals secrets. Daniel points the king to God and announces that the dream concerns “the latter days.”

f.w: there is a God in heaven that revealeth secrets

n: The king had been lying awake wondering about the future; God answered his very question through the dream.
Daniel insists he is not wiser than anyone else. The revelation came so the king could understand—a model of humility.

f.w: not revealed to me for any wisdom that I have

n: Daniel describes the dream: a huge, brilliantly shining statue with a terrifying appearance.

f.g: A statue.
Awe-inspiring, frightening.

n: The statue’s metals decline in value from head to feet: gold, silver, bronze.

f.g: Bronze.

n: Its legs are iron, and its feet a mix of iron and clay—strong but brittle.
A stone cut out “without hands”—not by any human effort—strikes the statue’s feet and shatters them. The weak point brings the whole thing down.

f.w: a stone was cut out without hands

n: The whole statue crumbles to dust, blown away like chaff, while the stone grows into a mountain that fills the earth. Latter-day Saints see this as the kingdom of God—the restored Church—rolling forth to fill the earth.

f.g: Husks separated from grain and blown away by the wind.

f.w: became a great mountain, and filled the whole earth

n: Daniel finishes describing the dream and turns to its meaning. “We” may include his three friends who prayed with him.
Daniel honors Nebuchadnezzar as “king of kings” but reminds him that God gave him his power.

f.g: A title of Babylonian and Persian emperors; ultimately it belongs to Christ.

n: God made Nebuchadnezzar ruler over people and creatures alike. “Thou art this head of gold”—Babylon is the first kingdom.

f.w: Thou art this head of gold

n: Two lesser kingdoms will follow. Many interpreters identify silver as the Medo-Persian Empire and bronze as Alexander the Great’s Greek empire.
The fourth kingdom is strong as iron, crushing everything. Many identify it with Rome, though some scholars see it as the Greek kingdoms that followed Alexander.
The fourth kingdom will become divided—strong like iron in some ways, weak like clay in others.

f.g: Mud or wet clay.

n: Partly strong and partly fragile, the kingdom will lack unity.
Alliances—perhaps through intermarriage—will try to bind the kingdom together, but iron and clay don’t bond.

f.w: they shall mingle themselves with the seed of men
f.g: Possibly royal intermarriages meant to create alliances.
Hold together.

n: The heart of the dream: during the time of these kings, God will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed or handed to others, and it will stand forever. Latter-day Saints believe this kingdom was restored through Joseph Smith in the last days.

f.w: shall the God of heaven set up a kingdom, which shall never be destroyed

n: The stone cut from the mountain without hands crushes all earthly kingdoms. Daniel declares the dream certain and its interpretation sure.

f.w: the stone was cut out of the mountain without hands

n: Overwhelmed, the king bows before Daniel and orders offerings and incense. Daniel had pointed him to God, but the pagan king responds in the only way he knows.

f.g: Incense.

n: Nebuchadnezzar confesses that Daniel’s God is the God of gods and Lord of kings—a remarkable acknowledgment, though not yet full conversion.

f.w: your God is a God of gods

n: Daniel is promoted to governor of the province of Babylon and head of all its wise men—echoing Joseph’s rise in Egypt.

f.w: made him ruler over the whole province of Babylon

n: Daniel does not forget his friends; at his request they are placed over Babylon’s administration. Daniel remains at the king’s court.

f.w: sat in the gate of the king
f.g: Served at the royal court, where officials conducted business.
